tldr: This paper organizes everyday contact-rich manipulation into eight core skills, introduces over 40 parts printable on consumer 3D printers with an aligned simulation suite, and uncovers key bottlenecks in modern vision and visual-tactile policies.
hero_caption: The eight core skill categories underlying everyday contact-rich manipulation. Grounded in observations of human tasks, they cover everything from grasping thin objects to placing under environmental constraints and regulating contact during tool use.
overview:
Recent robot learning has made remarkable progress thanks to large demonstration datasets and vision-language-action (VLA) models. However, most of these successes focus on 'visually obvious' tasks where object poses and appearances provide the primary cues. In contrast, many everyday activities require 'contact-rich' manipulation. These tasks demand modulating forces, exploiting environmental constraints, and reacting to changing contact states.

Prior contact manipulation research has concentrated narrowly on tasks like peg insertion or wiping. As a result, the field lacked a unified, reproducible benchmark for diverse everyday contact. To address this gap, the authors observed human daily manipulation and identified eight core skills. They then developed ContactBench 1.0, which features 36 reference tasks and over 40 standardized object assets. The physical assets use compliant spring mechanisms so they can be reliably fabricated on consumer 3D printers, paired with a simulator that offers tunable dynamic parameters.

On this benchmark, the authors evaluated leading vision-based policies like Diffusion Policy and $\pi_{0.5}$, along with modern visual-tactile policies. The results revealed that vision-only methods struggle to perceive contact, perform precise alignment, and avoid excessive forces. Surprisingly, existing tactile-equipped methods did not meaningfully improve performance either. This highlights fundamental challenges in sensor coverage and visual-tactile action integration.
contributions: Defining eight core skill categories that systematize contact-rich manipulation based on observations of everyday human tasks
Building over 40 open-source object assets and 36 evaluation tasks that can be reproducibly fabricated on consumer 3D printers while faithfully replicating realistic resistance loads
Developing an integrated simulation environment matched to the physical assets' dynamics, supporting tunable resistance loads and GelSight tactile sensing
Conducting real-world robot evaluations of recent vision-based and visual-tactile policies to quantitatively reveal vision-only limitations and tactile integration bottlenecks

sections.heading: Why Does Contact Remain a Major Hurdle for Generalist Manipulation?
sections.summary: While robot learning has advanced in vision-driven tasks, everyday manipulation relies heavily on contact skills like modulating force and exploiting constraints. This work identifies eight contact skills from human tasks and introduces a shared evaluation platform with 3D-printed assets and simulation.
sections.details:
To achieve general-purpose robot manipulation, recent research has leveraged large demonstration datasets and expressive policy models. Most of their successes, however, involve tasks where the next action can be inferred from visual cues like object appearance and poses.

Everyday tasks, by contrast, require sustaining appropriate forces, exploiting geometric constraints, and reacting instantly to contact transitions. Contact itself is the core mechanism for success. Prior work on contact-rich manipulation has mostly concentrated on isolated tasks like peg-in-hole or wiping, missing the breadth of everyday activities.

To address this, the authors carefully observed everyday human manipulation and extracted eight recurring skills often overlooked in robotics. They then created ContactBench 1.0 to systematically evaluate these skills. By open-sourcing 36 reference tasks and over 40 standardized assets, they enable laboratories worldwide to reproduce identical experiments.

sections.heading: Lineage of Simulation and Physical Benchmarks
sections.summary: Existing simulation environments and 3D-printable benchmarks have focused primarily on assembly or geometric variations. ContactBench stands out by covering broader everyday contact skills and allowing independent tuning of resistance forces without altering visual appearance.
sections.details:
### II-A Manipulation Simulation Benchmarks
Simulation environments like RLBench, robosuite, and ManiSkill have supported benchmarking through standardized task suites and GPU parallelization. Specialized setups have also emerged, such as UniDoorManip for door opening and Tactile Gym 2.0 with tactile simulation. However, they lack real-world counterpart assets whose contact behaviors can be freely tuned as parameters. The simulation suite in ContactBench maps one-to-one to printable physical mechanisms, allowing direct parametric control over contact resistance.

### II-B Reproducible Physical Assets and Benchmarks
Physical benchmarks generally either distribute commercial off-the-shelf hardware, like YCB and the NIST Task Board, or provide 3D printable designs, like FurnitureBench and Fabrica. The 3D printing route lets any lab build assets affordably. However, prior benchmarks often rely on generous clearances to prevent jamming, making it hard to generate the strong resistance loads needed for contact-rich tasks. Narrowing clearances to produce friction also makes resistance forces highly sensitive to printer-specific fabrication errors. ContactBench introduces compliant spring mechanisms that deliver consistent resistance loads independent of printer manufacturing variations.

sections.heading: Eight Contact Skills and Assets Built for Consumer 3D Printers
sections.summary: The benchmark organizes everyday contact tasks into eight skill categories, providing 36 tasks and over 40 assets. By incorporating internal PLA compliant springs, the assets accurately replicate realistic resistance forces regardless of the printer model used.
sections.details:
### III-A Eight Core Contact-Rich Skills
Based on observations of human tasks, the authors defined eight skills:
- Thin/Small Object Grasping: Requires sliding objects like cards or keys to table edges or flipping them up with fingertips.
- Multi-Object Grasping: Grasping multiple objects at once, like gathering scattered screws into the palm for efficiency.
- Cluttered Grasping (Clutter Picking): Singulating a target item from overlapping objects, such as stacked tableware or keychains, without collapsing the surroundings.
- Constrained Placement: Placing objects under constraints, like hanging on hooks or stacking on unstable piles, requiring precise alignment until the final release.
- In-Hand Relocation: Regrasping keys or USB sticks, or pivoting them against the environment to reorient them in-hand.
- External Contact Control: Regulating contact pressure or torque between a grasped object and the environment, such as erasing a whiteboard or tightening with a hex key.
- Articulated Manipulation: Moving doors, drawers, or switches smoothly along their kinematic joints without jamming.
- Insertion and Alignment: Beyond peg insertion, covers visually occluded alignments like threading screws or plugging into power sockets.

### III-B Benchmark Tasks and Task Variations
The benchmark includes 36 tasks: 31 short-horizon tasks testing 1-2 skills, and 5 long-horizon multi-stage tasks. To evaluate policy generalization, it introduces 'behavioral variations' (varying resistance loads or rotation angles while keeping visual appearance identical) and 'visual + behavioral variations' (varying geometry and scale).

### III-C 3D-Printed Asset Design and Validation
To ensure low-cost reproducibility, all assets use standard PLA filament and M3 screws. Instead of relying on tight part tolerances, assets incorporate internal spiral torsion springs and leaf springs using PLA elasticity. When fabricated across two printers (Bambu Lab P1S and Prusa XL) and measured with a wrist force sensor, a door handle required 5.01 N to 9.54 N of push force, closely matching a real door handle (5.45 N to 9.53 N). Force differences between printers stayed within 0.5 N, demonstrating high fabrication reproducibility.

Left shows the internal torsion spring of a door handle, and right shows the compression spring of an electrical outlet. They generate resistance through the elastic deformation of the plastic itself rather than part clearances.
captions.F3: Empirical force measurements comparing printed parts with real counterparts. Parts printed on different 3D printers (Bambu Lab P1S and Prusa XL) replicate realistic resistance levels of real door handles and outlets with minimal inter-printer variance.

sections.heading: Simulation Suite with Tunable Resistance and Tactile Rendering
sections.summary: A simulation suite physically aligned with the real assets was built on the Newton physics engine. Spring stiffness and preload can be tuned to match real force profiles, and it supports simulation of GelSight Mini tactile images and shear displacement.
sections.details:
### IV-A Asset and Contact Modeling
The simulation uses the Newton physics engine (with the MuJoCo Warp solver). Printed springs are modeled as prismatic or revolute spring-damper joints, exposing stiffness $K$ and preload $\tau_0$ as explicit parameters. This replicates realistic resistance forces without requiring expensive micro-deformation calculations. For contact-critical geometry like screw threads and keyholes, signed distance fields (SDFs) are used to balance computational speed and geometric fidelity.

### IV-B Tactile Sensing Simulation
The suite incorporates a sensor model of the GelSight Mini optical tactile sensor mounted on gripper fingertips. Using a hydroelastic pressure field formulation, it computes nonlinear indentation from normal surface contact and tracks shear displacement from relative tangential motion. The resulting deformation field is rendered with Taxim-based optical shading, generating tactile images that include marker displacements and surface height maps.

### IV-C Teleoperation and Scripted Policies
A teleoperation interface supports keyboard, gamepad, and SpaceMouse inputs, enabling data collection while monitoring end-effector contact forces in real time. The benchmark also provides scripted policies that automatically execute contact sequences—such as unlocking keys or push-and-turn dials—to generate seed demonstrations for training.

captions.F4: Overview of the ContactBench 1.0 simulation suite. (a) Kinematic modeling aligned with 3D-printed assets, (b) GelSight Mini tactile sensor simulation, and (c) teleoperation interface featuring real-time contact force visualization.
captions.F5: Tuning resistance on a simulated door handle. By adjusting spring stiffness $K$ and preload $\tau_0$, the simulation closely matches the force profiles of physical assets printed with different spring thicknesses.

sections.heading: Real-World Robot Evaluations: What Modern Vision and Tactile Policies Reveal
sections.summary: Using a UR5e robot, representative vision policies (DP, $\pi_{0.5}$) and tactile-augmented policies (RDP, FTP-1) were tested across six tasks. The best combination achieved only a 56.7% overall success rate, with tactile feedback offering no noticeable improvement.
sections.details:
### V-A Experimental Setup
A UR5e robot was fitted with a WSG50 parallel gripper, a wrist camera (RealSense D435i), and GelSight Mini tactile sensors. Four policies were evaluated: diffusion-based Diffusion Policy (DP) and large model $\pi_{0.5}$, alongside their tactile counterparts Reactive Diffusion Policy (RDP) and Foundation Tactile Policy (FTP-1). Six challenging tasks were chosen, including screw fastening, socket insertion, and door opening. Demonstrations were collected using a handheld gripper (UMI) tracked by a VIVE tracker, gathering 100 demonstrations per task and evaluating each method over 30 trials.

### V-B Four Failure Modes of Vision-Only Policies
Except for the door opening task (100% success), vision-based policies struggled across the board (achieving only 20% on socket insertion even with $\pi_{0.5}$). Analyzing failures revealed four common challenges:
- Failure to Establish and Maintain Contact: Policies failed to notice tools slipping in-hand during hex-key tightening and lost torque, or failed to flip up cards.
- Difficulty with Precise Alignment: When socket prongs were occluded from the wrist camera, policies could not perform small exploratory search motions after contact and jammed.
- Dangerous Excessive Forces: When misaligned, policies kept pushing forward, generating excessive forces exceeding 40 N in over half the trials across four tasks.
- Misidentifying Key States and Looping: Unable to visually distinguish a fully tightened screw from an incomplete one, policies repeated tightening motions endlessly and stalled.

### V-C Why Tactile Policies Did Not Save the Day
Evaluating RDP and FTP-1 with tactile inputs showed that success rates and completion times were virtually unchanged compared to base policies. Three key reasons explain this:
1. Limited Sensor Coverage: GelSight Mini sensors only cover the inner fingertip pads, failing to detect collisions on the back or sides of the fingers.
2. Inability to Learn Tactile-Driven Behaviors from Demonstrations: While humans use touch to guide exploratory alignment, policies failed to extract and reproduce these adaptive behaviors from demonstrations despite receiving tactile inputs.
3. Overreaction to Spurious Tactile Cues: During hex key tightening, normal in-hand slippage was misinterpreted as task completion, causing policies to terminate prematurely.

### V-D Case Study on Behavioral Generalization
When the rotation angle needed to open a door was increased from 60 degrees to 72 and 80 degrees, DP, $\pi_{0.5}$, and FTP-1 failed to increase wrist rotation, and their success rates dropped to near 0%. Only RDP adaptively increased wrist rotation, maintaining a 53.3% success rate at 80 degrees. This demonstrates that proper tactile integration can enable adaptation to unseen resistance variations. However, under a visual + behavioral variation where the knob diameter was reduced by 5 mm, all policies attempted to grasp at the original width, missed, and scored 0%.

captions.F8: The six representative tasks selected for real-robot evaluation along with human demonstration sequences. Tasks include nut engagement on threads, hex key fastening, socket insertion, door handle opening, chopstick retrieval, and card flipping/grasping.

sections.heading: Current Scope and Future Extensions
sections.summary: While this initial release focuses on rigid and articulated objects, future expansions will target deformable objects and fluids. Managing 3D print layer line artifacts on tactile sensors and systematically controlling friction are also key areas for future work.
sections.details:
ContactBench 1.0 was designed as a first step toward evaluating everyday contact-rich manipulation, focusing on rigid and articulated objects. Human environments, however, are full of deformable objects like clothing, as well as liquids and granular media. Supporting these will require extending physical assets, simulation methods, and evaluation protocols.

Moreover, while 3D printing provides great reproducibility, it introduces unique challenges. Micro-textures from 3D print layer lines appear distinctly on high-resolution tactile sensors like GelSight, potentially affecting sim-to-real and print-to-real transfer to commercial products. Furthermore, the benchmark currently lacks an explicit mechanism to systematically vary surface friction.

The authors envision expanding this benchmark beyond comparing policy algorithms into a comprehensive testbed for analyzing hardware mechanism design and tactile sensor placement and coverage.

sections.heading: Toward a Shared Foundation for Contact-Rich Manipulation
sections.summary: ContactBench 1.0 provides 36 tasks, over 40 3D-printed assets, and a tunable simulation suite categorizing everyday contact skills. It offers a standardized platform for labs worldwide to quantitatively benchmark physical interaction.
sections.details:
This paper introduced ContactBench 1.0, a new benchmark rooted in the observation of everyday human manipulation. It brings together eight core skill categories, 36 reference tasks, over 40 standardized 3D-printed assets, and a virtual simulation environment with tunable resistance loads and tactile simulation.

Validation across different 3D printers demonstrated consistent force reproduction, while detailed real-robot evaluations of modern policy learning methods highlighted the benchmark's utility. All physical 3D models and simulation code are open-sourced, establishing a shared foundation to accelerate future contact-rich robotic manipulation research.

sections.heading: Appendix: Simulation Modeling and Tactile Sensor Details
sections.summary: This section details how complex real-world mechanisms are approximated in simulation, and presents the mathematical model used to compute nonlinear indentation and shear deformation for the GelSight Mini.
sections.details:
### A-A Asset Mechanism Modeling
Rather than replicating full real-world CAD geometries, the simulation uses approximate models that preserve task-relevant contact behaviors and constraints. For example, a push-and-turn dial combines an axial prismatic spring joint with a pin-and-post gating slot, requiring sufficient axial push before turning. A key-and-cylinder mechanism incorporates an interlock constraint that only activates the deadbolt retraction joint when the key is inserted in the correct orientation to the specified depth.

### A-B Tactile Sensing Mathematical Model
The elastic gel pad on the fingertips follows a pressure-indentation relationship governed by local indentation $\delta$, gel thickness $h$, base stiffness $k_n$, and a strain-hardening parameter $\alpha$. Contact patches are rasterized into a normal pressure map $p_0(\mathbf{x})$ and normalized by the solver's normal force $F_n^{\mathrm{sim}}$. Tangential displacement $\mathbf{u}$ is updated from relative slip velocity $\mathbf{v}_\parallel$ and bounded by the Coulomb friction limit $\|\bm{\tau}\| = \|k_s \mathbf{u}\| \le \mu p$. Rendering this deformation field with a Taxim-based optical model enables high-fidelity simulation of normal surface features as well as shear forces and slip onset via marker displacements.

takeaways: Many everyday manipulation tasks are fundamentally contact-driven, causing vision-centric models to struggle with force regulation and fine alignment

Integrating internal compliant spring mechanisms into 3D-printed parts—rather than relying on clearance tolerances—enables consistent resistance forces (high reproducibility) regardless of 3D printer differences
Simply adding tactile sensors does not automatically improve performance; broader sensor coverage and fundamentally better learning frameworks for translating touch into action are needed
Behavioral variations (where resistance or rotation angles change without visual cues) can be handled through adaptive generalization when tactile feedback is integrated properly
limitations: Current assets are limited to rigid and articulated objects, leaving out contact manipulation of deformable objects like garments or fluids
Micro-textures from 3D printing layer lines appear distinctly on tactile sensors, potentially hindering policy transfer to real commercial products
Systematic mechanisms to adjust and control surface friction coefficients are not yet fully incorporated
